summary: JSON Web Signature (JWS) represents content secured with digital signatures or Message Authentication Codes using JSON-based data structures. The cryptographic algorithms it uses are described in the separate JSON Web Algorithms specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7515 defines JSON Web Signature (JWS), a format for protecting content with a digital signature or message authentication code. It defines compact and JSON serializations and rules for producing and validating them.

questions: what is a json web signature
what is the difference between jws compact and json serialization
what does the alg header parameter do in jws
subtitle: A JSON-based format for protecting content with a digital signature or message authentication code.

tldr.problem: Applications need a standard way to protect arbitrary content from undetected modification using digital signatures or message authentication codes.
tldr.mechanism: JWS combines a header, payload, and signature or MAC. Its compact form uses three base64url-encoded parts; its JSON form can represent multiple signatures.
tldr.outcome: A JWS lets a recipient check integrity and, with a digital signature, the origin under the selected key. Cryptographic algorithms are specified separately in JWA.

today: RFC 7515 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2015. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it; RFC 7518 defines its algorithms.

sections.title: What a JWS Represents
sections.content:
JSON Web Signature (JWS) represents content protected by a digital signature or Message Authentication Code (MAC). The protection covers an arbitrary sequence of octets, not only JSON content.

The specification defines a compact URL-safe serialization and a JSON serialization. Cryptographic algorithms and their identifiers are defined separately in the JSON Web Algorithms specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A JWS lets a recipient check whether protected content has changed. The content may be any sequence of bytes, even when the JWS itself uses JSON-related formats.

sections.title: Headers, Payload and Signature
sections.content:
A JWS contains a JOSE Header, a payload, and a signature or MAC. The protected header contains parameters covered by the signature; an unprotected header is allowed only in the JSON serialization and is not covered.

The signing input is the base64url-encoded protected header, a period, and the base64url-encoded payload. The algorithm named by the alg header parameter creates or verifies the signature. An unsecured JWS uses alg value none and provides no integrity protection.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature covers the protected header and payload together. A JWS with an unprotected header does not protect those header values.

sections.title: Compact and JSON Serializations
sections.content:
Compact Serialization joins three base64url-encoded parts with exactly two period characters: protected header, payload, and signature. It supports one signature or MAC and has no unprotected header.

JSON Serialization represents the payload and signature information as JSON members. Its general form supports multiple signatures or MACs, while its flattened form supports one. Applications specify which serialization features they use.
sections.plainLanguage: The compact form is one string with three parts separated by two periods. The JSON form uses named members and can represent multiple signatures.

sections.title: Header Parameters
sections.content:
Header parameter names must be unique. The alg parameter is required and must be understood. Optional parameters can identify a key, declare a type, or describe the payload's content.

The crit parameter lists extensions the recipient must understand. It must appear in the protected header, must not be empty, and cannot list parameters that do not occur in the JOSE Header. New parameter names should be registered or use collision-resistant names.
sections.plainLanguage: The header identifies the algorithm and may provide information about a key or content type. A critical extension must be understood by the recipient or the JWS is invalid.

sections.title: Producing and Validating a JWS
sections.content:
To produce a JWS, an application creates the payload and header, encodes the protected header and payload with base64url, signs the signing input, and encodes the signature. The JSON form repeats the signature steps for each signature or MAC.

To validate, a recipient parses the serialization, decodes the protected header, checks that it is valid UTF-8 JSON, checks required parameters, and verifies the signature with the algorithm named by alg. At least one signature must validate in a multi-signature JWS, and the application must decide which algorithms it accepts.
sections.plainLanguage: Creating a JWS means encoding the protected header and payload, then signing their combined input. A recipient decodes the parts and verifies the signature before accepting the protected content.

sections.title: Identifying the Key
sections.content:
A recipient must determine which key was used to sign or authenticate the content. Header parameters such as kid, jwk, x5c, and key-set URLs can provide key information; another application-defined method may also be used.

Key-identification parameters must be integrity protected when they affect a trust decision. URLs used to retrieve keys or certificates must use TLS, and the server identity must be validated. Key exchange for shared symmetric keys is outside this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipient needs the correct key to verify a JWS. Key hints that influence trust must themselves be protected, and retrieval URLs require TLS.

sections.title: Keys, Algorithms and Replay
sections.content:
The RFC recommends at least 128 bits of entropy for keys and requires private signing keys and MAC keys to be protected. A MAC proves that the message came from a party holding the shared key; it does not prove origin to a third party.

Implementations must validate that the algorithm used matches alg and should protect the algorithm parameter from substitution. Applications can limit replay by including a unique message identifier in protected content. JSON must be strictly validated, including rejecting malformed input and duplicate header names.
sections.plainLanguage: JWS security depends on strong, protected keys and strict validation of the named algorithm and JSON. Applications that need replay protection must include and check a unique identifier themselves.

sections.title: Header and Media Type Registries
sections.content:
The RFC creates an IANA registry for JSON Web Signature and Encryption Header Parameters. New names require a specification and expert review. It recommends keeping registered parameter names short when practical.

The RFC also registers application/jose for compact JWS or JWE and application/jose+json for JSON serialization.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry gives implementations a shared list of header parameter names. The two media types identify compact and JSON serializations.
